newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan of Ghana leads for U.N. top post.
newsitem.headline: Annan of Ghana leads for U.N. top post.

text.p: Kofi Annan of Ghana, the U.N. official in charge of peacekeeping, on Wednesday emerged as the only viable candidate so far in the race for U.N. secretary-general, but he still faced a veto from France.

The Security Council conducted three unofficial ballots on Wednesday and two on Tuesday with Annan ending up as the only candidate to get more than the required nine votes. But each time the votes against him included one by a permanent member, which diplomats said was France.

Paris envoys were backing Ivory Coast Foreign Minister Amara Essy, a former president of the U.N. General Assembly, who remained in second place, ending up on Wednesday with six votes. He was opposed in each ballot by two council members with vetoes, which diplomats said were the United States and Britain.

Council President Paolo Fulci of Italy, who said another vote would be taken on Thursday, told reporters: "No conclusive result has yet been reached and therefore the straw poll goes on for the four names that you already know. He also said no new names had been submitted so far.

Diplomats said the next step might be high-level discussions to persuade France to change its mind or possibly to throw the race open to Asian nominee if the contest on African candidates remains deadlocked.

The other two candidates in the balloting, Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, and Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, a former U.N. special envoy for Burundi, never approached the required nine votes. Both also were opposed by the United States and Britain, envoys said.
France, the United States, Britain, Russia and China have veto power on the 15-member Security Council. The council's choice of a candidate must be endorsed by the 185-member General Assembly.

Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's five year term ends on Dec. 31. He withdrew temporarily from the race after a veto by the United States, but the council agreed to follow tradition and give preference to another African candidate.
The vote at the end of the fifth round of balloting was:
-- Annan - 11 in favour, 4 against, including one negative vote from a a veto-bearing permanent member.
-- Essy - 6 to 4, including two negative votes from permament members.
-- Algabid - 3 to 9, including two negative votes from permanent members
-- Ould-Abdallah - 2 to 10, including two negatives votes from permanent members.
The contest is rapidly developing into a test of wills between the United States and Britain against France.

Annan, the undersecretary-general for U.N. peacekeeping operations, speaks French, has worked for the United Nations in Geneva and studied there at the Institut Universitaire des Hautes Etudes Internationales.

But he does not come from a French-speaking country and he is widely considered the candidate favoured by the United States. And France is believed to resent the U.S. veto last month of Boutros-Ghali, who obtained the support of all 14 other council members in a Nov. 19 vote in which he was the sole candidate.

Washington says the United Nations needs new leadership to carry out reforms. It also favours a candidate whose command of English could influence not only the largely English-speaking press corps in New York but also a sceptical U.S. Congress.

Paris not only championed Boutros-Ghali's election for an initial five-year term in 1991 but was widely perceived as having used its influence to ensure his victory by out-manoeuvring other council members, including the United States and Britain.
Although Boutros-Ghali "suspended" his candidacy on Dec. 4 and did not figure in the balloting, he has not withdrawn from the race.
